title: WHY DAVID’S KINDNESS STARTED A WAR
paragraphs:
WHY DAVID’S KINDNESS STARTED A WAR
He Sent Comfort. They Saw a Conspiracy. And What Happened Next Reveals Something Terrifying About the Way We Can Respond to Grace.
Sometimes a war does not begin with hatred.
Sometimes it begins with kindness offered to someone who has become too suspicious to receive it.
A king had died.
His son was grieving.
David heard the news and decided to do something remarkably human.
He would send comfort.
No invasion.
No threat.
No ultimatum.
No army marching toward the border.
Just men carrying condolences to a grieving son.
And before the story was over, those men would be publicly humiliated, armies would mobilize, thousands of soldiers would enter the conflict, and what began as an act of kindness would become war.
But here is the part that should make us uncomfortable.
The kindness was not the problem.
The interpretation of the kindness was.
And somewhere inside this ancient story may be a frightening picture of something we still do today.
We become wounded enough to distrust love.
Proud enough to reject correction.
Suspicious enough to question mercy.
Ashamed enough to attack the hand reaching toward us.
And sometimes we become so accustomed to expecting betrayal that when grace finally arrives at our door...
we treat it like an enemy.
That is where the story begins.
Second Samuel 10 tells us that the king of the Ammonites died and his son Hanun became king in his place.
David remembered Hanun's father, Nahash.
So David said:
“אֶעֱשֶׂה־חֶסֶד”
’e‘eseh-chesed.
“I will show kindness.”
That Hebrew word matters.
חֶסֶד — chesed.
It is one of the richest words in the Old Testament. Depending upon its context, it carries ideas of kindness, loyalty, steadfast love, covenant faithfulness, mercy, or faithful devotion.
David was not announcing war.
He was expressing chesed.
Second Samuel 10:2 records his intention:
“אֶעֱשֶׂה־חֶסֶד עִם־חָנוּן בֶּן־נָחָשׁ כַּאֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה אָבִיו עִמָּדִי חֶסֶד”
In context:
“I will show kindness to Hanun son of Nahash, as his father showed kindness to me.”
So David sent servants to comfort Hanun concerning the death of his father.
Picture the scene.
Hanun has inherited a throne while burying a father.
Grief and power have arrived almost simultaneously.
Then representatives from Israel appear.
They have come because David remembers kindness and intends to answer kindness with kindness.
But before Hanun can simply receive the gesture, voices gather around him.
His officials begin whispering.
Do you really believe David sent these men because he honors your father?
Do you really believe they came to comfort you?
Maybe they are spies.
Maybe they are studying the city.
Maybe David intends to overthrow you.
The biblical text records their suspicion plainly.
The men carrying consolation are reinterpreted as men carrying conspiracy.
Nothing in the passage tells us that David secretly sent them as spies.
The stated intention is chesed and consolation.
Yet Hanun listens to suspicious counsel.
And this is where an ancient political disaster suddenly becomes painfully personal.
Because some of us know exactly what suspicion can do to a human heart.
Someone loves you...
and you search for the hidden motive.
Someone apologizes...
and you assume manipulation.
Someone tries to correct you...
and you hear condemnation.
Someone reaches toward you...
and every wound from your past screams, “Don't trust them.”
Sometimes those instincts exist because people really have betrayed us. Scripture never requires gullibility, and biblical wisdom does not mean pretending evil does not exist.
But discernment and cynicism are not the same thing.
Discernment seeks truth.
Cynicism has often already decided what the truth must be.
Hanun had David's messengers standing in front of him.
But he allowed other men's suspicions to tell him what those messengers supposedly meant.
Then suspicion became humiliation.
Hanun seized David's servants.
He shaved off half their beards.
He cut their garments so severely that they were exposed.
Then he sent them away.
Read that slowly.
They arrived carrying sympathy.
They left carrying shame.
They came to comfort a grieving king.
They returned humiliated by him.
The text says the men were:
“נִכְלָמִים מְאֹד”
nikhlamim me’od.
Deeply, exceedingly humiliated.
And David's response to his humiliated servants is one of the quietest beautiful moments in the chapter.
He did not immediately parade their shame before everyone.
He sent people to meet them.
Then he told them to remain in Jericho until their beards had grown back.
Then they could return.
There is tenderness hidden inside that command.
David gave humiliated men somewhere to recover.
He did not demand that they walk immediately back into public view while carrying visible evidence of what had been done to them.
He gave dignity time to heal.
Someone reading this needs that sentence.
Dignity sometimes needs time to heal.
Maybe somebody humiliated you.
Maybe something was exposed.
Maybe people laughed at the chapter of your life that nearly destroyed you.
Maybe your marriage collapsed publicly.
Maybe your addiction became known.
Maybe your failure became somebody else's conversation.
Maybe you made the mistake yourself and now you cannot escape the memory of who you were.
There are wounds that bleed privately and wounds that make you afraid to show your face again.
David looked at humiliated men and effectively told them:
Stay here until you are ready to return.
And centuries later, the Gospel reveals a King infinitely greater than David who receives ashamed people without delighting in their humiliation.
Jesus does not deny our sin.
He deals with it more seriously than we do.
But He does not save sinners by pretending they were never guilty.
He saves sinners by bearing what their guilt deserves.
That is why the cross is simultaneously horrifying and beautiful.
At Calvary, God's holiness is not discarded so mercy can survive.
Justice and mercy meet.
Sin is exposed as deadly.
Grace is revealed as astonishing.
And the innocent Son of God willingly bears the shame of sinners.
Jesus was mocked.
Stripped.
Beaten.
Rejected.
Publicly humiliated.
Crucified.
The One who had no sin entered the place of shame for people drowning in it.
Hebrews tells us that Jesus endured the cross, “despising the shame.”
The King entered our disgrace so redeemed sinners could someday stand before God clothed not in their own righteousness, but in His.
That is why Christianity is not self-improvement with religious vocabulary.
It is rescue.
But return to Hanun for a moment.
Because his tragedy becomes worse.
After humiliating David's servants, the Ammonites realize they have made themselves offensive to David.
And here was the moment when everything might have changed.
Imagine if Hanun had stopped.
Imagine if he had admitted:
I listened to the wrong voices.
I misjudged David.
I humiliated innocent men.
I was wrong.
Scripture does not record him doing that.
Instead, the Ammonites hire military forces.
Their fear of consequences drives them deeper into conflict.
This is one of sin's oldest patterns.
We do wrong.
Then instead of confession, we defend it.
Instead of repentance, we recruit excuses.
Instead of surrender, we build armies around our pride.
One lie requires another.
One hidden message requires another hidden message.
One compromise needs another compromise to protect it.
One secret browser history becomes a carefully guarded life.
One affair becomes layers of deception.
One bitterness becomes an entire theology explaining why forgiveness is impossible.
One wounded ego begins collecting people who will agree that we were justified.
And eventually we are no longer merely protecting ourselves from other people.
We are protecting our sin from the truth.
That is when grace begins to feel threatening.
Not because grace is cruel.
Because grace asks us to stop pretending.
This is where Hanun's story becomes more than history.
It becomes a mirror.
How many wars inside us began because we refused to say three words?
“I was wrong.”
How many relationships died because pride considered apology more painful than separation?
How many years have people spent running from God because they assumed His call to repentance was an attempt to destroy their lives?
The enemy has been repeating variations of the same lie since Eden:
God cannot really be trusted.
His command is keeping something good from you.
His boundaries are oppression.
His truth is hostility.
His authority threatens your freedom.
And when that lie enters the human heart, we begin treating the God who gives life as though He were the enemy of life.
That is the tragedy of sin.
Sin does not merely make us guilty.
It distorts what we love, what we trust, and sometimes even how we interpret the goodness of God.
We begin calling chains freedom and freedom chains.
We hide from the only One who can cover our shame.
We run from the Physician because admitting sickness feels unbearable.
We reject the Savior because accepting salvation requires admitting we cannot save ourselves.
And still...
God comes near.
That is the scandal of grace.
Not that God looks at rebellion and calls it harmless.
He doesn't.
Not that repentance is optional.
It isn't.
Not that judgment is imaginary.
It isn't.
The scandal is that the holy God against whom we have sinned made the way for sinners to be reconciled to Himself through His Son.
“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son...”
Jesus did not come merely to make decent people slightly nicer.
He came seeking the lost.
He called sinners to repentance.
He touched the unclean.
He ate with people respectable society despised.
He forgave.
He restored.
And then He walked deliberately toward Jerusalem knowing what waited there.
The cross.
Our culture can make the cross decorative because we have seen it on walls, necklaces, buildings, books, and screens.
But crucifixion was scandalous.
Humiliating.
Violent.
Public.
The Roman cross was not originally jewelry.
It was an instrument of execution.
And Christianity makes the staggering proclamation that the sinless Messiah willingly went there.
Paul writes in Greek:
Christos hyper hēmōn apethanen.
“Christ died for us.”
Romans 5:8 places that declaration inside something breathtaking: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Not after we repaired ourselves.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we erased the history.
While sinners.
That is grace.
But grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
The Jesus who forgives also calls us to follow Him.
The Gospel announces forgiveness and creates a new allegiance.
Repentance is not paying God back for mercy.
You could never pay Him back.
Repentance is the turning of a heart that has finally stopped defending the very thing from which Christ came to rescue it.
And perhaps that is why this story hurts.
David's servants came carrying kindness.
Hanun received them as threats.
What are you doing with the grace God is putting in front of you?
Do not answer quickly.
What if the conviction you have been trying to silence is mercy?
What if the Scripture that disturbed you was not God pushing you away, but God exposing the thing destroying you?
What if the Christian who lovingly confronted you was not necessarily your enemy?
What if your exhaustion comes partly from maintaining defenses God never asked you to build?
What if you have spent years fighting a war against surrender?
You know the secret.
You know the bitterness.
You know the habit.
You know the relationship.
You know the pride.
You know what you keep deleting.
You know what happens when nobody is watching.
You know the version of yourself presented at church and the version that appears behind a locked door.
And perhaps you have become extremely good at explaining it.
But explanations cannot wash away sin.
Jesus can.
This is where the story can change.
Hanun's chapter shows what happens when suspicious pride keeps escalating.
Your chapter does not have to end there.
Because you can repent.
Right here.
No performance.
No religious theater.
No carefully polished Christian vocabulary.
Just truth.
“Jesus, I have sinned.”
There are few sentences pride hates more.
And few sentences grace makes safer to say.
First John teaches that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse.
The Gospel does not tell you to hide until you become worthy enough to return.
It tells you that Christ is the only sufficient Savior.
Come into the light.
Turn from sin.
Trust Christ.
Stop building armies around what Jesus died to free you from.
And if you have wandered far from God, do not confuse the distance you have traveled with the distance His grace is capable of reaching.
Peter denied Jesus.
Thomas doubted.
Paul had persecuted Christians.
The thief beside Christ had no lifetime left in which to manufacture an impressive religious résumé.
Scripture is crowded with people whose stories would have looked hopeless if God had stopped writing where human failure put the period.
That is why we keep saying:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by rewriting history as though your sin never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by changing God's standard.
Jesus rewrites the sinner's future through redemption.
Guilt can become forgiveness.
Rebellion can become repentance.
Bondage can become freedom.
The runaway can come home.
The ashamed can be restored.
The spiritually dead can be made alive.
The enemy can become family.
The scandal does not have to be the final sentence.
Grace can write what sin never could.
And maybe this article did not find you simply so you could press “like,” feel something for thirty seconds, and continue scrolling.
Maybe somebody you know is living like Hanun.
Suspicious of God.
Wounded.
Defensive.
Building armies around a heart that is secretly terrified.
Maybe someone on your Facebook friends list is one sleepless night away from giving up.
Maybe they would never walk into a church today.
But they might read something you shared.

If you want your life to glorify God, one practical way is to use what He has entrusted to you, including your voice and your reach, to point people toward Christ. You cannot know whose screen this might reach at exactly the moment they are finally ready to stop running.
Love them. Pray for them. Let the tag mean, “I thought of you, and I want you to know there is still grace.”
There are truths you understand differently when the night gets darker.
And if this exposed something hidden in you, do not hide behind silence.
You do not owe strangers the details of wounds that should remain private. But there is something powerful about believers refusing to pretend that discipleship means never struggling.
We need communities where repentance is not entertainment, broken people are not gossip material, and testimony is not reserved for people whose scars are already neat enough for a stage.
It does not.
Not because financial support earns salvation.
It never could.
Jesus purchased redemption. We don't.
Not to prove your faith.
Not to purchase God's approval.
Not because clicking “share” makes anyone righteous.
Someone is misreading God's conviction as rejection.
Someone thinks they have sinned too badly to return.
Someone is exhausted from protecting a secret.
Someone is surrounded by voices telling them not to trust the King.
Someone is shaving the messengers, so to speak, because receiving grace feels more frightening than continuing the war.
And maybe God can use your ordinary act of sharing biblical truth to place one message in front of them:
You can stop fighting.
You can repent.
You can come home.
Christ receives sinners who come to Him in faith.
The cross is sufficient.
The tomb is empty.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
And grace is still calling.
David sent kindness and Hanun heard conspiracy.
God sent His Son, and humanity crucified Him.
Yet even the cross we made into an instrument of rejection became, according to God's saving purpose, the place where redemption was accomplished.
Think about that.
Human beings gave Jesus a cross.
God raised Him from the dead.
Sin wrote scandal.
Grace answered with an empty tomb.
So perhaps the most dangerous question is not whether you have ever failed.
You have.
So have I.
The question is what you will do when grace stands at the gate.
Will you keep listening to the voices telling you to run?
Will you keep defending what is destroying you?
Will you keep hiding behind religion, success, humor, anger, lust, achievement, relationships, money, ministry, or pride?
Or will you finally surrender?
Because the war does not have to continue.
The King you have been running from is the only One who can save you.
And perhaps the grace you have spent years fearing is the very grace that has been pursuing you home.
Do not spend your life fighting the hands that were pierced to bring you home.
